results.content: Homepage/Smart Lending/Risk Simulation. # Risk Simulation. Optimise your credit strategy with prospective analysis of portfolio risk. to do a complete stress test on 100% of the credit portfolio. monitoring of credit portfolio based on regulatory credit risk measures. ## The solution for the analysis of portfolio prospective risk under adverse conditions. Risk Simulation is an **advanced platform** for doing **stress analysis** on credit portfolio and predicting the effect on capital and profitability. You can do **simulations based on macroeconomic scenarios** with differentiated levels of severity, analyse the effect of the different scenarios on credit risk parameters (e.g. PD, LGD), and regulatory measures (e.g. RWA, ECL), while also **meeting the governance and monitoring requirements** provided for by the EBA-LOM guidelines. * Do **basic and dynamic simulations** guided by standard or customized assumptions. * Consult **interactive dashboards** with insights that help you evaluate the effect of scenarios on capital measures and credit risk. * Compare the results of the different simulations, archive them, and create **summary reports**. A portfolio divided into various analytical aspects. A solution based on consolidated Cerved models and algorithms. A flexible tool that adapts to scenarios different from Cerved ones. What is the difference between basic and dynamic simulations? Basic simulations are based on standard assumptions, with non-configurable parameters, using macroeconomic scenarios with preset weight and Cerved econometric models to generate Forward-Looking, PD and LGD curves. Dynamic simulations, on the other hand, are customized "what-if" assumptions, which can set up one or more parameters simultaneously. What data can be displayed with the dashboards? You can display the expected trend on regulatory outputs (RWA, ECL) and risk parameters (PD, LGD), compare the simulated values with the current/threshold values defined by the bank, and analyse the different results got through past and current simulations. For each risk index, it is also possible to have an overview and create in-depth analyses divided by subject type, geographical area, rating, staging, technical form, etc. ## Analyse risk from a forward-looking perspective with Risk Simulation. results.title: IRRBB Rate Shock Scenarios for Effective Risk Management
results.content: # IRRBB Rate Shock Scenarios for Effective Risk Management. A key tool in managing IRRBB (see Understanding IRRBB) is the use of interest rate shock scenarios. Regulators and banks use these scenarios to measure how changes in interest rates (parallel shifts, twists in the yield curve, etc.) would affect the economic value of equity (EVE) and net interest income (NII) of the banking book. ### BCBS-Prescribed IRRBB Shock Scenarios (and 2024 Updates). The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) introduced a standardized set of IRRBB shock scenarios in its 2016 guidelines, establishing six interest rate shock scenarios (applied currency-by-currency) to capture both parallel and non-parallel yield curve movements (six scenarios for EVE sensitivity, two parallel scenarios for NII sensitivity):. Under the original 2016 calibration (using data from 2000–2015), the prescribed shock for USD had a parallel shock of 200bp, a short-rate shock of 250bp, and a long-rate shock of 150bp, which are used to calculate the different scenarios according to the BCBS prescribed formula, with certain floors (minimum shocks of 100bp for low-rate currencies) and caps (maximum shocks of 400bp for parallel and 500bp short-term for high-volatility currencies). In July 2024, after a period of consultation (and after the March 2023 events), the BCBS finalized an update to the IRRBB shock scenario calibration (to be implemented in 2026). relative changes, replacement of the global shock factors with local shock factors, higher confidence level), the calibration dataset was extended from 16 years to 24 years, which now capture the sharp rate hikes of 2022–2023 (as opposed to the "lower for longer" in the original window), see BCBS-Recalibration of shocks in IRRBB. ### Industry Practices in Calibrating Rate Shock Scenarios. While regulators prescribe standard scenarios as a baseline, banks often develop (or should) internal interest rate shock and stress scenarios tailored to their risk profiles. Using the BCBS scenarios as a starting point many banks use additional scenarios (larger shocks, different shapes, etc.) to fully capture their unique risk profile. \* Note: While the BCBS-IRRBB framework incorporates some of this optionality with the use of multipliers (0.8, 1.2 applied to different assumptions and rate scenario) the solution methodology tends to fall short (or is not always implemented).

results.title: Bending the Curve: How Curve Methodology Transforms ECL Assessment in Stress Testing
results.content: By modeling **Prepayment Probability (PP)**, **Probability of Default (PD)**, **Loss Given Default (LGD)**, and **Exposure at Default (EAD)** as time-dependent curves, we can achieve greater accuracy and responsiveness in stress testing exercises. **Curve methodology** refers to modeling risk parameters such as PP, PD, LGD, EAD and other components as continuous or time-dependent functions, rather than static values, reflecting their evolution over the life of a financial product. SAS Stress Testing includes the **ST Curves models**, namely ***ST Curves Common –***  and ***ST Curves –*** , which are designed to assess expected credit losses (ECL) under a range of stress scenarios using curve methodology. To support curve modeling, SAS Stress Testing Solution uses an *analysis data set* – often referred to as the **risk factor curve data set** – that contains the monthly evolution of each risk component for a portfolio or segment. By modeling PD, LGD, EAD, and PP as dynamic term structures, institutions can derive time-sensitive loss expectations that are critical for both informed risk management and regulatory stress testing.

results.title: IFRS 9 vs Basel III: How Credit Risk Metrics Differ | Islam Monged CISA, CISM, CAMS posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.content: Here's a quick comparison: 🔹 IFRS 9 ▪ Purpose: Financial reporting ▪ Perspective: Point-in-Time (PIT) ▪ Macroeconomic adjustment: Mandatory ▪ PD: Forward-looking, includes economic forecasts ▪ LGD: Reflects expected recovery, discounted ▪ EAD: Behavioral assumptions applied ▪ Use: Expected Credit Loss (ECL) provisioning 🔹 Basel III ▪ Purpose: Regulatory capital adequacy ▪ Perspective: Through-the-Cycle (TTC) ▪ Macroeconomic adjustment: Not required (except in stress testing) ▪ PD: Long-run average, cycle-neutral ▪ LGD: Often includes downturn stress scenarios ▪ EAD: Conservative estimation with regulatory Credit Conversion Factors ▪ Use: Capital requirement (Unexpected Loss) calculation 💡 IFRS 9 models are more sensitive to current conditions, while Basel III models are more conservative and stable over time. ✅ Key benefits: - Stable, long-run LGD anchor for unsecured portfolios - Smooths noise from individual cases and economic cycles - Supports better risk planning, stress testing, and capital allocation - Enhances IFRS 9 compliance by combining PIT variability with long-term experience 💭 Unsecured loans pose unique challenges due to limited collateral, and methods like Chain Ladder help bridge data gaps, enabling more accurate, forward-looking ECL estimates.
